extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary theory and aesthetics; poets, critics, and writers seeking classical foundations for composing and evaluating poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_short: evaluating and composing poetry and drama
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains classical/aesthetic criteria (Aristotle, Plato, Coleridge, Goethe) for composing and judging poetry and fine art: what poetry should aim to express, how plots and characters ought to be formed, the proper end of art, and how audience and moral function bear on artistic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry approaches the universal
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry 'approaches nearer to the universal' and is nearer to philosophy because it reveals a higher truth by expressing the universal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The universal in poetry is presented through sensuous imagery and imaginative treatment rather than as abstract proposition; poetry expresses the universal as seen through concrete, sensuous representation, not as a pure abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express the universal through the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of poetry is 'to represent the universal through the particular' — to give a concrete and living embodiment of a universal truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The universal should be particularised to sense and presented as a living organism whose parts relate structurally to the whole; this is not allegory (where an abstract idea is embodied in one example) but artistic generalisation of a particular case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Particulars must be generalised by artistic treatment (not mere allegory)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poetic method is not to embody a general idea in a particular (allegory), but for the particular case to be generalised and become universal by artistic treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge and Goethe: the poet receives sensuous impressions and must 'artistically round them off' so that others receive the same impression; avoid flattening characters into mere emblems or abstractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot composition: outline general idea first, then fill with detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle advises that the poet should 'set forth his plot in its general idea (ἐκτίθεσθαι καθόλου)' — abstracting accidental time/place/person features — and afterwards fill it with incidents and proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes this as a distinct compositional order (useful whether drawing on tradition or invention) but questions its practical/poetical value; treat it as a method, not an absolute rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should be representative yet particularised
rubrics_metrics.description: Persons in poetry must be 'clothed with generic attributes' representative of a class, but those class characteristics are 'so modified and particularised' that individuality and life remain distinct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coleridge's warning: do not mistake 'representative of a class' for an endorsement of abstraction — class traits should be probable given situation and richly particularised (Shakespearian example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Involution of the universal in the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should 'involve' the universal within the individual form — unlike geometry (where universal truth is uppermost), in poetry the individual form is uppermost though the universal shines through.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that the universal is not singular or abstract but 'all the truths that meet in the individual'; poetic truth is the multiple universals instantiated in the individual case.

rubrics_metrics.name: End of fine art: to give pleasure (rational enjoyment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: the end of the fine arts is to give pleasure (πρὸς ἡδονήν) — a form of rational or elevated enjoyment connected with leisure (διαγωγή) and akin to the delight of speculative thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes higher (rational/aesthetic) pleasures from mere pastimes; fine art's pleasure is a characteristic, elevated mode of enjoyment, not simple amusement or utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish higher vs lower pleasures in judging art
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts and forms afford pleasures of varying quality; music or literature may serve as pastime or as a noble rational enjoyment depending on form and audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating, do not conflate popular/childish pleasures (toys, pastime) with the higher aesthetic pleasure appropriate to cultivated audiences; the higher pleasure is the proper end of fine art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's proper end is the pleasure of the spectator (ideal listener), not the maker
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle regards the end of art as the pleasurable impression produced upon the spectator or listener; the artist's satisfaction is incidental — the decisive end is the effect on the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should focus on the work's effect on a normally constituted, cultivated human audience rather than on the creator's inward gratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: The ideal (cultivated) spectator is the standard of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'free and educated listener' or man of cultivated taste (ὁ χαρίεις) functions as the 'rule and standard' for judgments of art; the cultivated public, not specialized artisans, is the appellate standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different audiences enjoy different things; critical judgment should appeal to the cultivated public's sensibilities rather than purely popular or purely specialist verdicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: A tragedy's test: capacity to awaken pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic action must possess an inherent capacity to call forth pity and fear; the poet must impress this quality on the dramatic material, and the degree to which it does so is the test of artistic merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All Aristotelian rules for tragedy (plot construction, ideal hero, recognition) flow from this primary requirement; avoid contrivances that undermine the tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not pander to audience weaknesses (avoid false happy endings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic poets are tempted to produce happy endings to gratify audience weakness, but such endings do not afford the characteristic tragic pleasure and therefore corrupt the art's distinctive end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating dramatic choices, penalize devices that substitute an inauthentic or popular pleasure for the art's distinctive emotional function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy and lower arts rank as pastimes; judge them by appropriate standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy and lower forms of art are akin to pastime (παιδιά) and their pleasure is of a lower, sportive kind; they fit men for serious work rather than constituting the highest aesthetic end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not apply the same evaluative standard reserved for serious/tragic art to comedy or playful arts; recognise the different function and distinctive pleasure of each form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry's moral/educational function
rubrics_metrics.description: A long tradition (Homer, Plutarch, Eratosthenes) holds that poetry has a direct moral purpose — the poet as teacher whose work 'affords correction in morals' and serves as a 'preparatory school of philosophy.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation can legitimately consider whether a work instructs or shapes character; critics historically insisted poets should be 'good men' and poetry should prepare readers for philosophical truths, especially for general audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's objective form and subjective effect are intertwined
rubrics_metrics.description: Although an artwork's end might be conceived as realization of a true idea (εἶδος) in form/matter, Aristotle recognises that the attainment of that end is known by the hedonistic (pleasurable) effect on the percipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging completeness/perfection, consider both formal realization (form impressed on matter; internal coherence) and the enduring, universal element of the subjective pleasure it produces in properly constituted audiences.
